quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The harbour ferry has been replaced by an electric boat that charges overnight at the quay. Passengers notice the quiet first, since there is no engine rumble or diesel smell. The crossing takes the same time as before, and tickets cost no more. The operator says running costs are lower, which is why it plans to convert the second ferry next year.
options: The electric ferry crosses faster but costs passengers more.
Passengers complained about the silence of the new electric boat.
An electric ferry is quieter and cheaper to run.
The operator has already converted both of its ferries.
quests.correctAnswer: An electric ferry is quieter and cheaper to run.
quests.hint: Separate what has already happened from what is only planned.
quests.explanation: The paragraph lists benefits of the first electric ferry and gives a reason for converting the second. Wrong options reverse the time and cost facts, invent a complaint or treat the plan as completed.
keyPoints: An electric boat replaced the diesel harbour ferry.
Journeys and ticket prices are unchanged, but it is quiet and clean.
Lower running costs have led to plans to convert a second ferry.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A mobile library van visits remote villages every two weeks. The librarian brings picture books for children, large-print novels for older readers and a few laptops for people without internet. Some villagers wait at the roadside for an hour before it arrives. One farmer says the van's visit is the highlight of his fortnight, since he also gets to chat with neighbours.
options: A library van gives remote villagers books, internet and company.
Farmers borrow the laptops to sell their produce online.
The van visits each village daily and brings fresh books.
Villagers avoid the van because it takes an hour to arrive.
quests.correctAnswer: A library van gives remote villagers books, internet and company.
quests.hint: Choose the option that covers the service and its value to people.
quests.explanation: The van supplies materials for different readers and provides social contact. Wrong options exaggerate its frequency, reverse villagers' reaction or invent a use of the laptops.
keyPoints: A library van visits remote villages fortnightly.
It carries books for all ages and laptops for internet access.
Villagers value it as a chance to meet neighbours.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Volunteer translators help refugees complete forms at the town hall. Many forms use legal language that even native speakers find confusing, and mistakes can delay housing or benefits. The translators explain each question in plain words before writing the answers with the applicant. Officials say the number of rejected applications has fallen since the service began.
options: Native speakers find legal forms easier than refugees do.
Refugees now complete official forms unaided, since the service has ended.
Officials rejected more applications after the service began.
Volunteer translators cut mistakes on official forms for refugees.
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteer translators cut mistakes on official forms for refugees.
quests.hint: Trace the problem, the help and the measurable result.
quests.explanation: The service tackles language barriers and results in fewer rejected applications. Wrong options remove human help, reverse the comparison or reverse the trend.
keyPoints: Volunteers help refugees fill in complicated town hall forms.
They explain the questions in plain words.
Rejections have fallen since the service started.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A breakfast club opens at seven-thirty each morning in Northgate Primary. Children who arrive early can eat toast, porridge or fruit for a small donation, and those who cannot pay eat for free. Teachers noticed that late arrivals dropped and that pupils were more attentive before break. The head teacher says the club feeds friendships as well as stomachs.
options: Teachers started the club because pupils were too attentive.
Friendships are the main reason children join the club.
A breakfast club helps children eat and arrive punctually.
Children at Northgate must pay before they may eat breakfast.
quests.correctAnswer: A breakfast club helps children eat and arrive punctually.
quests.hint: Keep the food, the effect on lessons and the social side together.
quests.explanation: The club supplies food and leads to better punctuality, attention and friendships. Wrong options reverse the payment rule, invent a motive or reduce it to one reason.
keyPoints: A breakfast club serves food from seven-thirty for a small donation.
Pupils who cannot pay eat for free.
Lateness fell, attention improved, and friendships grew.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Along the coast, volunteers are planting mangrove seedlings in muddy shallows. The tangled roots slow waves, so storms cause less damage to villages behind them. Fish and crabs also shelter among the roots, which helps local fishers. Planting is slow work, and about a third of seedlings do not survive, but each year the green belt grows wider.
options: Mangrove planting protects villages and supports fishing, with slow progress.
Fishers plant mangroves to keep crabs out of their nets.
Most mangrove seedlings survive their first year in the mud.
Waves have become stronger because of the growing roots.
quests.correctAnswer: Mangrove planting protects villages and supports fishing, with slow progress.
quests.hint: Include both the benefits and the limitation mentioned.
quests.explanation: Mangroves protect the coast and support fishers, though many seedlings die and progress is slow. Wrong options reverse the survival rate, the fishers' purpose or the effect on waves.
keyPoints: Volunteers plant mangrove seedlings along the coast.
The roots slow waves and shelter fish and crabs.
About a third die, yet the green belt grows each year.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: On a former car park, neighbours have built a city farm with raised beds, chickens and a small orchard. Local schools visit to learn where food comes from, and surplus vegetables go to a nearby food bank. The land belongs to the council, which has agreed to lease it for ten years. Organisers hope a longer lease will allow them to build a greenhouse.
options: The council has sold the land to the neighbours outright.
Schools buy vegetables from the farm each week.
A greenhouse has already been built on the car park.
A city farm educates children and feeds people.
quests.correctAnswer: A city farm educates children and feeds people.
quests.hint: Note who owns the land and what has been achieved versus hoped for.
quests.explanation: The farm serves education and a food bank, but the land is leased and the greenhouse is only a hope. Wrong options change ownership, invent sales or treat a hope as a fact.
keyPoints: Neighbours turned a car park into a city farm.
Schools visit and surplus food goes to a food bank.
The council leases the land for ten years, and a longer lease is hoped for.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: An online marketplace for second-hand books lets readers list titles they no longer need. Buyers pay only postage plus a small fee, and sellers receive the rest. Students find it especially useful for textbooks, which can cost hundreds when bought new. Critics note that popular titles sell quickly while older editions may wait months for a buyer.
options: Textbooks sell more slowly than other books, according to critics.
A second-hand book marketplace saves students money.
Sellers must pay the postage plus a large fee.
Critics say the marketplace makes new books cheaper.
quests.correctAnswer: A second-hand book marketplace saves students money.
quests.hint: Look for the benefit and the criticism together.
quests.explanation: The marketplace lowers costs, especially for students, but not all books sell quickly. Wrong options reverse who pays fees, misplace the slow sellers or misuse the critics' view.
keyPoints: Readers list unwanted books on an online marketplace.
Buyers pay only postage and a small fee, which helps students.
Popular books sell fast, but older editions can wait months.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A clinic in the highlands introduced a phone app that lets patients describe symptoms with photos and short messages. A nurse reviews each request and decides whether the patient needs a visit or can be helped by phone. This has reduced the number of long trips over rough roads. Some older patients still prefer to visit in person, and the clinic respects that choice.
options: Patients must use the app before seeing a nurse, though some object.
The app replaced the clinic's nurses with automatic diagnosis.
Older patients have stopped visiting the clinic altogether.
An app helps a clinic treat patients remotely.
quests.correctAnswer: An app helps a clinic treat patients remotely.
quests.hint: Check whether an option turns a choice into a rule.
quests.explanation: The app reduces unnecessary journeys but does not remove the option to visit. Wrong options make the app compulsory, remove nurses or say older patients stopped visiting.
keyPoints: A highland clinic uses an app for symptom photos and messages.
Nurses decide whether to help remotely or invite the patient in.
Fewer long trips are needed, but people can still visit.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When a rail strike shut the main line for a week, commuters improvised. Some carpooled, others cycled and a few negotiated to work from home. An employer survey later found that productivity barely changed. One manager admitted that the week had made her question whether so many people needed to travel five days a week, though she added that not every job could be done remotely.
options: A rail strike showed that commuting can be reduced.
Most commuters refused to change how they travelled.
Productivity fell sharply during the week of the strike.
The manager decided that jobs can be done remotely in her whole company.
quests.correctAnswer: A rail strike showed that commuting can be reduced.
quests.hint: Include the evidence and the caution in the last sentence.
quests.explanation: The week revealed flexibility in commuting, and the manager's remark includes a limit. Wrong options reverse the productivity finding, overextend the manager's conclusion or contradict commuters' response.
keyPoints: A weeklong rail strike forced commuters to adapt.
People carpooled, cycled or worked from home.
Productivity barely changed, but not all jobs can be done remotely.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A small software company decided to hire people without university degrees. Applicants complete a two-day practical test instead of submitting a certificate. The company found that several successful candidates had learned coding through online courses and had strong problem-solving skills. Some staff worried about the training required, but managers say the results justify it.
options: Successful candidates mostly learned coding at university.
The company now rejects applicants who have university degrees.
Skills tests helped a company find programmers without degrees.
Staff welcomed the plan and expected little extra training.
quests.correctAnswer: Skills tests helped a company find programmers without degrees.
quests.hint: Pay attention to what replaced the degree requirement.
quests.explanation: The practical test replaced the certificate and revealed capable self-taught candidates. Wrong options exaggerate the change, reverse staff worries or contradict how candidates learned.
keyPoints: A software company stopped requiring degrees.
Applicants take a two-day test showing practical skills.
Self-taught candidates performed well, and training is judged worth it.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some young people choose apprenticeships instead of university. They earn a wage while learning and finish without student debt. However, apprenticeships can limit career choices, since training is tied to one employer's methods. University graduates may earn more over a lifetime, but they face years of study before earning anything. Advisers say the better path depends on the person's goals.
options: Apprenticeships and university each suit different goals.
University graduates start earning while they are still studying.
Apprenticeships lead to higher lifetime earnings than university degrees.
Advisers say everyone should choose university over other routes.
quests.correctAnswer: Apprenticeships and university each suit different goals.
quests.hint: Decide whether the writer picks a winner or shows a trade-off.
quests.explanation: The paragraph compares two routes and concludes that individual goals matter. Wrong options declare one route always better, reverse who earns during study or misstate advisers' view.
keyPoints: Apprentices earn while learning and avoid debt.
Their training can be narrow and tied to one employer.
Graduates may earn more later but study first, and advisers say goals decide.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A design firm allows staff to choose their own hours as long as they attend the Tuesday team meeting. Early risers finish by three, while night owls start at noon. Managers feared that projects would slip, but deadlines have been met more often than before. Staff turnover has dropped, and the firm now uses flexibility as a selling point when recruiting.
options: Deadlines were missed more often after the change.
Flexible hours improved deadlines and helped staff retention.
Managers dislike flexibility and plan to end it soon.
Staff must work between nine and five on most days, with Tuesdays free.
quests.correctAnswer: Flexible hours improved deadlines and helped staff retention.
quests.hint: Check what managers expected and what actually happened.
quests.explanation: Managers worried about delays, but results were positive and staff stayed. Wrong options reverse the schedule rule, the deadline result or managers' attitude.
keyPoints: A design firm lets staff set their own hours except for a Tuesday meeting.
Deadlines were met more often despite managers' fears.
Fewer staff leave, and flexibility helps recruiting.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: At a large company, every new employee is paired with a mentor from a different department. The pairs meet monthly to talk about career goals, office culture and any problems. Mentors say they learn as much as their partners, since younger colleagues bring fresh ideas. The scheme is voluntary, yet most staff choose to take part.
options: Newcomers gain from the meetings, while mentors gain little.
A mentoring scheme helps newcomers and mentors learn.
Mentors must come from the same department as newcomers.
The company requires employees to join the scheme in their first month.
quests.correctAnswer: A mentoring scheme helps newcomers and mentors learn.
quests.hint: Note who benefits and whether participation is compulsory.
quests.explanation: The scheme connects departments, and mentors gain as well as newcomers. Wrong options reverse the pairing rule, ignore mentors' learning or make participation compulsory.
keyPoints: New employees are paired with mentors from other departments.
They meet monthly to discuss goals, culture and problems.
Mentors also learn, and most staff join voluntarily.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A telecom company used to answer customer complaints within a week. Then it discovered that customers who waited more than two days were far more likely to cancel. The company hired extra staff and introduced a rule that every complaint must receive a reply within twenty-four hours. Cancellations dropped, and the cost of hiring was covered by the customers it kept.
options: Cancellations increased after the twenty-four-hour rule.
The company answered complaints in two days before the change.
Faster complaint replies kept customers and paid for staff.
Customers who waited a week were most likely to stay.
quests.correctAnswer: Faster complaint replies kept customers and paid for staff.
quests.hint: Trace the finding, the decision and the financial result.
quests.explanation: Data showed that delay caused cancellations, so quicker replies retained customers and covered costs. Wrong options reverse the finding, change the old response time or reverse the result.
keyPoints: The company answered complaints within a week.
It found that longer waits caused cancellations.
A twenty-four-hour reply rule reduced cancellations and paid for extra staff.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A furniture maker's deliveries were delayed when a shipment of timber was stuck at a foreign port. Rather than wait, the owner contacted local sawmills and bought smaller batches at a higher price. Customers received their orders only a few days late, and the company avoided cancelling contracts. The owner has since arranged two suppliers so that one problem cannot stop production again.
options: A furniture maker solved a delay and reduced future risk.
The company now depends on a single supplier again.
The owner waited for the foreign shipment and cancelled contracts.
Local sawmills sold timber to the owner at a lower price.
quests.correctAnswer: A furniture maker solved a delay and reduced future risk.
quests.hint: Find the response to the problem and the lesson taken from it.
quests.explanation: The owner acted quickly to keep orders going and then reduced future risk. Wrong options reverse the action, the price or the supplier plan.
keyPoints: A timber shipment was stuck at a foreign port.
The owner bought smaller batches from local sawmills.
Two suppliers now protect against future delays.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: During the heatwave, several schools sent pupils home early because classrooms exceeded thirty degrees. Teachers said concentration disappeared after lunch. The education department has now offered grants for shades, fans and reflective roof paint. Parents' groups welcome the money, although they say the cost of cooling schools properly will be much higher than the grants.
options: The education department has paid for air conditioning in the hottest schools.
Teachers said concentration improved after lunch.
Schools closed for the whole heatwave because of the heat.
Hot classrooms prompted grants that parents call insufficient.
quests.correctAnswer: Hot classrooms prompted grants that parents call insufficient.
quests.hint: Look for the response and the reaction to it.
quests.explanation: Overheated classrooms led to grants that parents welcomed but consider limited. Wrong options exaggerate the closure, overstate the grants or reverse concentration.
keyPoints: Hot classrooms sent pupils home early during a heatwave.
The department offers grants for shades, fans and reflective paint.
Parents welcome the grants but say more money is needed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Factory workers in the metal plant now wear earplugs fitted to each person's ear. Ordinary foam plugs often fall out, and workers took them off to hear instructions. The new plugs let speech through but block harmful noise. Hearing tests after a year showed no further loss among those who used them, and complaints about communication have almost disappeared.
options: Workers now remove the earplugs to hear instructions.
Custom earplugs protect factory workers' hearing while allowing conversation.
Hearing tests showed further loss after the first year.
Foam earplugs stay in better than custom earplugs.
quests.correctAnswer: Custom earplugs protect factory workers' hearing while allowing conversation.
quests.hint: Identify the old problem and how the new item solves it.
quests.explanation: Custom plugs solve the problem of comfort and communication and protect hearing. Wrong options reverse the fit, the test results or the workers' behaviour.
keyPoints: Foam earplugs fell out and were removed to hear instructions.
Custom plugs block harmful noise but let speech through.
Hearing loss stopped, and communication complaints faded.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A sugar tax on soft drinks began two years ago. Manufacturers responded by cutting sugar in their recipes, and sales of the least sugary drinks rose. The tax also raised money, which the government spent on school sports equipment. Critics argue that the tax hits poorer families hardest, though supporters reply that healthier drinks are now cheaper than they were.
options: The government spent the tax money on new hospitals.
Supporters say healthier drinks have become more expensive.
A sugar tax changed recipes but raised fairness concerns.
Manufacturers increased sugar in recipes to protect their sales.
quests.correctAnswer: A sugar tax changed recipes but raised fairness concerns.
quests.hint: Include the effect and the disagreement.
quests.explanation: The tax altered manufacturers' choices and funded sports, but critics dispute who pays. Wrong options reverse the recipe change, misname the spending or reverse supporters' point.
keyPoints: A sugar tax on soft drinks began two years ago.
Manufacturers reduced sugar, and the tax paid for school sports equipment.
Critics say poorer families are hit hardest; supporters point to cheaper healthier drinks.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Glaciers in the mountain valley have shrunk by a third in fifty years. Meltwater currently feeds the river that supplies farms downstream, so summer flows are high. Scientists warn that once the ice is much smaller, the river will run dry in late summer. Farmers are therefore being encouraged to plant crops that need less water and to build small reservoirs.
options: Shrinking glaciers help rivers now and threaten later shortages.
Farmers have stopped growing crops downstream from the glaciers.
The river is already dry in late summer in the valley.
Glaciers have grown by a third over fifty years.
quests.correctAnswer: Shrinking glaciers help rivers now and threaten later shortages.
quests.hint: Keep track of what is true now and what is expected later.
quests.explanation: Melting currently increases flows but will reduce them, so farmers need to adapt. Wrong options reverse the glaciers' change, treat a future risk as present or exaggerate farmers' response.
keyPoints: Valley glaciers have shrunk by a third in fifty years.
Meltwater keeps the river high for now.
Scientists expect late-summer shortages, so farmers are adapting.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Marine biologists have found that some corals survive warmer water better than others. They are moving heat-tolerant fragments to damaged reefs and watching whether they grow. Early results are encouraging, though the process is expensive and slow. Experts stress that transplanting corals cannot replace efforts to slow global warming, which is the underlying cause of the damage.
options: Corals have been shown to survive warming of several degrees.
Transplanting corals is quick and cheap to do.
Transplanting heat-tolerant corals helps reefs and does not solve warming.
Experts say warming is a minor cause of reef damage.
quests.correctAnswer: Transplanting heat-tolerant corals helps reefs and does not solve warming.
quests.hint: Watch the final sentence, which sets a limit on the claim.
quests.explanation: The project offers hope but does not tackle the cause. Wrong options exaggerate corals' resilience, reverse the cost and speed or deny the cause.
keyPoints: Some corals tolerate warm water better than others.
Biologists move tolerant fragments to damaged reefs.
Results are encouraging, but warming remains the underlying problem.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The city collects food scraps from homes in small brown bins. Trucks take the scraps to a facility where they are turned into compost and biogas. The biogas powers part of the facility, and the compost is given to local farmers. At first, residents complained about smells, but weekly collections and tighter lids have solved most of the problems.
options: Residents put food scraps in green bins at the facility.
Food scraps are collected and converted into compost and energy.
Complaints about smells have increased with weekly collections.
Farmers pay the city for the compost it produces.
quests.correctAnswer: Food scraps are collected and converted into compost and energy.
quests.hint: Follow the scraps from the kitchen to the final products.
quests.explanation: Scraps become compost and biogas, and design changes reduced smell complaints. Wrong options change the bin, the payment or the effect of collections.
keyPoints: The city collects household food scraps in brown bins.
Scraps become compost for farmers and biogas for the facility.
Weekly collection and better lids reduced smell problems.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A paper mill now makes writing paper from used cartons and office waste. The recycled pulp needs more sorting, so production is a little slower, but the mill saves thousands of litres of water each week. Customers were sceptical at first about the quality. After trying samples, many schools switched, since the paper feels almost the same and costs less.
options: Schools prefer the recycled paper because it looks different.
The mill has stopped using cartons and office waste.
Recycled paper takes more water to produce than new paper.
Recycled paper saves water and is now accepted by schools.
quests.correctAnswer: Recycled paper saves water and is now accepted by schools.
quests.hint: Include the benefit and how attitudes changed.
quests.explanation: The mill's process saves water and, after sampling, customers accepted it. Wrong options reverse the water comparison, the materials or the reason schools switched.
keyPoints: A mill makes paper from used cartons and office waste.
It is slightly slower but saves much water.
After trying samples, many schools switched.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The amateur theatre group in Millbrook performs one play every autumn in the old grain store. Members build the sets, sew costumes and handle the lights themselves. Ticket money covers materials, and any surplus goes to the village hall. Last year, the group tried a musical for the first time, and it sold out all five nights, so this year's plan is even more ambitious.
options: The group hires professionals to build sets and sew costumes.
The musical failed to attract audiences last year.
A village theatre group produces shows and aims higher.
Ticket money is paid to the members as a salary.
quests.correctAnswer: A village theatre group produces shows and aims higher.
quests.hint: Look at what members do themselves and how last year affects this year.
quests.explanation: The group does all the work itself, funds the show from tickets and plans more after a successful musical. Wrong options reverse the workforce, the money's use or the musical's result.
keyPoints: Millbrook's amateur group performs one play every autumn.
Members make the sets, costumes and lighting.
A sold-out musical has encouraged bigger plans.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Kavita took up photography after a health scare made her want to spend more time outdoors. She began with her phone and moved to a second-hand camera when she noticed how much she enjoyed noticing small details. Now she walks the same park each dawn and posts one picture a day. Followers say her photos make them notice their own neighbourhoods differently.
options: Photography gave Kavita a reason to explore outdoors.
Kavita photographs models in studios each dawn.
Kavita started photography to earn money from her followers.
Kavita explores a different park each morning.
quests.correctAnswer: Photography gave Kavita a reason to explore outdoors.
quests.hint: See how the hobby began and what it has become.
quests.explanation: A health scare led to a hobby that changed how Kavita and her followers see familiar places. Wrong options change the setting, the motive or the routine.
keyPoints: A health scare encouraged Kavita to spend more time outdoors.
She progressed from phone photos to a second-hand camera.
Her daily park pictures help followers notice their own surroundings.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Linguists estimate that a language disappears somewhere in the world about every two weeks. Most of these languages are spoken by small communities whose children have moved to bigger languages for school and work. Recording elders and creating children's books can help, and some communities have revived their languages successfully. However, revival requires years of steady effort, not a single project.
options: Languages disappear when communities record their elders.
Languages are vanishing, and revival takes long effort.
Large languages are replacing children's books.
A single project is enough to revive a language.
quests.correctAnswer: Languages are vanishing, and revival takes long effort.
quests.hint: Check which claim the writer qualifies at the end.
quests.explanation: The paragraph explains why languages vanish and what can help, with a caution that revival takes time. Wrong options reverse cause and effect, misplace the books or ignore the caution.
keyPoints: A language disappears about every two weeks.
Children in small communities often switch to bigger languages.
Recording and books can help, but revival takes years.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Residents in the northern valley speak a dialect that outsiders find hard to follow. Some parents worried that their children's accents would hurt them at job interviews, so they encouraged standard speech. However, a local radio station now airs programmes in the dialect, and teenagers have begun mixing it into songs. Elders say they are pleased to hear it in new places.
options: Outsiders follow the valley dialect on the radio without difficulty.
Elders are upset that teenagers use the dialect in songs.
Parents now punish children for speaking the dialect.
A local dialect is being valued again.
quests.correctAnswer: A local dialect is being valued again.
quests.hint: See how attitudes change in the second half.
quests.explanation: Fear of discrimination led parents to discourage the dialect, but radio and music are bringing it back. Wrong options reverse the outsider comment, the elders' reaction or parents' behaviour.
keyPoints: Northern valley residents speak a dialect that outsiders find difficult.
Some parents feared accents would harm job chances.
Radio and teenagers' songs are now reviving the dialect.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The Rivas family decided to hold a wedding without expensive extras. They invited sixty guests instead of two hundred, cooked the food themselves and asked friends to lend flowers from their gardens. The savings paid for a longer honeymoon. Guests said the day felt more personal, and several couples have since planned smaller ceremonies of their own.
options: A smaller, homemade wedding felt more personal and inspired others.
The Rivas family spent more on their wedding than most.
Guests missed the extras that were left out.
The savings were spent on hiring caterers.
quests.correctAnswer: A smaller, homemade wedding felt more personal and inspired others.
quests.hint: Compare the choice, the result and the influence.
quests.explanation: The family's choices reduced costs, made the event personal and inspired other couples. Wrong options reverse the spending, guests' reaction or how the food was provided.
keyPoints: The Rivas family had a smaller wedding with sixty guests.
They cooked and borrowed flowers instead of paying for extras.
Guests found it personal, and other couples followed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Every June, residents of Cedar Lane close the street for a neighbourhood festival. Each household brings a dish or performs, from dancing to poetry. The event began ten years ago when two families argued over parking, and a mutual friend suggested a picnic to calm things down. It became a tradition that now draws visitors from nearby streets.
options: A picnic that eased a dispute became a lasting tradition.
The festival began when two families won a parking contest.
The festival started last year with dance performances.
Residents of neighbouring streets are excluded from the festival.
quests.correctAnswer: A picnic that eased a dispute became a lasting tradition.
quests.hint: Trace how an event started and what it turned into.
quests.explanation: A picnic to settle a disagreement grew into an annual celebration. Wrong options reverse the origin, restrict attendance or misplace the start date.
keyPoints: Cedar Lane holds a street festival each June.
It began ten years ago as a picnic to calm a parking dispute.
It has grown into a tradition with visitors from other streets.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A bookshop near the university keeps a large ginger cat named Marmalade. Students often visit just to stroke him, and many buy a paperback while they are there. The owner admits that the cat sleeps through most of the day and once knocked over a display. Even so, sales are higher on days when Marmalade sits in the window.
options: Marmalade is an energetic cat who attracts customers throughout the day.
Sales are lowest when the cat sits in the window.
Students avoid the shop because the cat knocks over displays.
A lazy shop cat still draws customers.
quests.correctAnswer: A lazy shop cat still draws customers.
quests.hint: Include the cat's flaws and the surprising effect.
quests.explanation: The cat's charm brings sales even though he is not very active and makes mistakes. Wrong options reverse the students' reaction, the cat's energy or the sales pattern.
keyPoints: A bookshop keeps a ginger cat named Marmalade.
Students visit to stroke him and often buy a book.
Sales rise when he sits in the window, despite his sleepiness.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Night-shift nurses at the district hospital struggle to sleep after work because daylight keeps them awake. The hospital gave them blackout curtains and eye masks, and a sleep specialist ran a short workshop on routines. After three months, nurses reported longer, deeper sleep, and errors on late shifts declined. The hospital plans to offer the same package to cleaners and porters who also work nights.
options: Cleaners and porters have already received the sleep package.
Sleep support improved night nurses' rest and reduced errors.
Blackout curtains were given to the sleep specialist but not to the nurses.
Night shifts were cancelled after nurses reported many errors.
quests.correctAnswer: Sleep support improved night nurses' rest and reduced errors.
quests.hint: Separate what has been done from what is only planned.
quests.explanation: The package helped nurses sleep, and better sleep is linked to fewer late-shift errors. The plan for cleaners and porters is still in the future, so treating it as done is a mistake.
keyPoints: Night nurses had trouble sleeping in daylight.
The hospital provided curtains, masks and a routine workshop.
Sleep improved and errors declined, and other night staff may get the same help.
